records.sourceFile: Return to play after rotator cuff tear in National Football League athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Lapica HE, Burgmeier RJ, Ravich JW, Schurhoff MR, Vargas LA. Return to Play After Rotator Cuff Tear in National Football League Athletes. JSES International. 2023.
paper.abstract: Publicly available data were used to identify 29 NFL players (mean age 27.4 years) who sustained a rotator cuff tear between 2000 and 2019. Return to play (RTP) was defined as being on an active roster for at least one regular-season game after treatment. Twenty-three of 29 players (79%) returned, after an average of 198 days. Players who returned were younger and had shorter pre-injury careers, and return rates did not differ between operative and nonoperative treatment.
paper.tldr: About 8 in 10 NFL players in this small series returned to play after a rotator cuff tear. Players who did not return were older (mean 30.3 vs 26.7 years) and had longer careers, and return rates did not differ between surgery and nonoperative care in this cohort of 29.
paper.methods: Retrospective case series using publicly available NFL injury reports, play-by-play documents, and player statistics. A position-specific performance score was normalized per game and compared before and after injury, with each player serving as his own control. Groups were compared with Mann-Whitney U tests and binomial proportions with 95% confidence limits.
paper.findings: Twenty-three of 29 players (79%; 95% CI 59.2% to 89.4%) returned to play, after an average of 198.4 days, and returners had a mean performance score ratio of 1.0. Non-returners were older (30.3 vs 26.7 years, p=0.02), 4 of the 6 were over 30, and they had longer pre-injury careers (7.5 vs 4.0 years, p=0.01). Return rates did not differ between operative (19/24) and nonoperative (4/5) players (p=0.95), and time to return was 259.5 days after surgery compared with immediate return in the nonoperative group (p=0.001).
paper.limitations: Data came from third-party public sources, not medical records, so diagnosis, tear size and pattern, and surgical details are unknown. The authors state the sample is likely underpowered, and the reasons for not returning could not be determined. The performance score excludes offensive linemen. Table IV lists a career length of 23.0 years for players at other positions, which conflicts with the text (about 3 years) and is likely a reporting error. The operative vs nonoperative return-rate P value is .95 in the Results text but .97 in Table II.
paper.practicalImplications: For NFL players with a rotator cuff tear, this series supports counseling around a return rate of about 8 in 10. Older, veteran players returned less often, so the authors advise counseling players over 30 about that risk. Treatment type did not separate outcomes here, but the sample is too small to choose between surgery and nonoperative care.
paper.athleteDev: This study describes career outcomes after injury rather than training or testing. It is useful for roster and career-stage planning for veteran players, since older players returned less often, but it does not inform training prescription.
paper.rtp: Use this study to counsel NFL players after a rotator cuff tear: about 79% returned in this series, and those who did not return were older on average, with 4 of 6 over 30. It cannot be used to choose between surgery and nonoperative care, predict an individual player's recovery, or estimate outcomes in non-NFL athletes.

records.sourceFile: Return to play after shoulder                                 instability in National Football League          athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Okoroha KR, Taylor KA, Marshall NE, Keller RA, Fidai M, Mahan MC, et al. Return to play after shoulder instability in National Football League athletes. J Shoulder Elbow Surg. 2018;27:17-22.
paper.abstract: Eighty-three NFL players who sustained an in-season shoulder instability event between 2006 and 2014 were compared with matched control players who had no such injury. Return to play (RTP), time to RTP, recurrent instability, games played and treatment type were recorded. Overall, 92.8% of players returned to regular-season play. Players who had surgical repair had fewer recurrent instability events and a longer interval before any recurrence, and RTP games per season fell after injury.
paper.tldr: Most NFL players with an in-season shoulder instability event returned to play. Players who had surgery had fewer repeat episodes, but they missed much more time before returning.
paper.methods: Retrospective cohort study using publicly available internet injury reports verified against NFL.com. Players were included if they had been drafted and had played at least one NFL game before the instability event. Injured players were compared with age-, size-, position- and experience-matched NFL controls. Categorical variables were compared with chi-square or Fisher exact tests and continuous variables with t tests or Wilcoxon rank sum tests.
paper.findings: Of 83 players, 77 (92.8%) returned to regular-season play, and 36 of these 77 (46%) had a recurrent instability event. Among those who returned, the surgical group had a lower recurrence rate (26% vs 55%, P=.021) and a longer median recurrence-free interval (14.7 vs 2.5 weeks, P=.050). Median time to RTP was 39.3 weeks operatively and 2.3 weeks nonoperatively (P<.001), and nonoperative subluxations returned faster than dislocations (0.0 vs 3.0 weeks, P=.029) but recurred sooner (1.5 vs 5.0 weeks, P=.044). Returners played about 1.5 fewer games per season than before injury (P=.014), but games, seasons and Pro Bowls after return did not differ from matched controls.
paper.limitations: The data came from third-party internet sources, which may contain inaccuracies and may miss some players. Treatment was not randomized, and players were more likely to have surgery if injured later in the season or on the right arm; instability direction and surgical procedure were not recorded. The abstract and conclusion say subluxations are more likely to recur, but the Results report no difference in recurrence incidence between dislocations and subluxations, only a shorter time to recurrence. The abstract reports 92% and 47%, while the Results give 92.8% and 46%; the Results figures are used here.
paper.practicalImplications: For NFL players with an in-season shoulder instability event, the study supports counseling that most will return, with a high chance of repeat instability. Surgery was associated with fewer repeat episodes and longer intervals, but it also meant a much longer time to return. The drop in games per season after return did not differ from matched controls, so it should not be presented as an injury-specific loss.
paper.athleteDev: The study tracks games played per season before and after instability, but post-return games and seasons did not differ from matched controls. Its career and game-count findings are descriptive and do not provide training or performance prescriptions.
paper.rtp: Use this study to set return expectations for NFL players after a shoulder instability event: most returned, but nearly half of returners had a recurrence. It cannot establish that surgery prevents recurrence in an individual athlete, and it does not provide clearance criteria or return timelines for non-NFL athletes.

records.sourceFile: Return to play rates in NFL wide receivers and running backs after ACL reconstruction - An updated analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Manoharan A, Barton D, Khwaja A, Latt LD. Return to Play Rates in NFL Wide Receivers and Running Backs After ACL Reconstruction: An Updated Analysis. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;9(1):2325967120974743.
paper.abstract: Publicly available NFL injury reports from the 2009-2010 to 2015-2016 seasons were used to identify running backs (RBs) and wide receivers (WRs) who underwent ACL reconstruction. Return to play (RTP) was defined as playing at least one NFL game after reconstruction. Overall, 61.8% of players returned, at a mean of 13.6 months. The RTP group had more career games before injury, and WRs who returned had decreased performance after reconstruction compared with matched uninjured controls.
paper.tldr: Fewer than two-thirds of NFL running backs and wide receivers returned to a game after ACL reconstruction in this 2009 to 2016 window. Wide receivers who returned produced less after injury than matched uninjured controls.
paper.methods: Retrospective descriptive study using publicly available injury reports, team rosters, and statistics sites. RTP was defined as playing at least one NFL game after reconstruction. Pre- and postinjury position-specific statistics were compared with paired t tests, and returners were compared with matched controls (same position, same team where possible, with 4 healthy seasons) using unpaired t tests.
paper.findings: Of 76 players, 47 (61.8%) returned to play (64.5% of RBs and 60% of WRs), at a mean of 13.6 months (median 12 months for RBs, whose mean was inflated by one 47-month return). RTP players had more career games before injury (72.2 vs 40.1, P=.0128). In the performance analysis (36 returners), WR receptions per game fell from 2.86 to 1.95 (P=.0013), yards per reception from 12.71 to 9.92 (P=.0143) and receiving touchdowns per season from 3.71 to 2.12 (P=.0011), and all three were lower than controls after injury. RB yards per rush fell from 4.45 to 3.42 (P=.0044), but no RB measure differed from controls after injury.
paper.limitations: The study is retrospective and based on public sources, so concomitant meniscal or cartilage injuries, surgical technique and rehabilitation protocols are unknown. The control group was designed to match opportunity, not to represent a true intervention. The Results and Discussion describe RB performance as a non-significant drop, but Table 2 reports a significant fall in yards per rush (P=.0044), so the table values are used here. Reasons for not returning are not known, and results apply only to RBs and WRs with successful return.
paper.practicalImplications: Counseling for RBs and WRs after ACL reconstruction should allow for a return rate near 6 in 10 and a recovery period of about 12 to 14 months. Wide receivers who return may have lower production, so expectations for their post-injury output should be realistic. The RB decline in yards per rush is a measured finding, but the lack of change in rushes per game limits what can be concluded about overall role.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use the before-and-after statistics to set realistic expectations for production in the season after an ACL reconstruction, especially for wide receivers. The study measures game statistics, not physical capacity, so it does not guide training or testing.
paper.rtp: Use this study to counsel NFL running backs and wide receivers about return rates (about 62%) and typical timelines (12 to 14 months) after ACL reconstruction. Timelines partly reflect the season calendar rather than readiness alone, and the study cannot predict an individual player's return, define clearance criteria, or be applied to other positions or leagues.

records.sourceFile: Platelet-Poor Plasma for the Treatment of Acute Hamstring Muscle Injuries in Collegiate Football Athletes - A Cohort Study.pdf

paper.citation: Kruse RC, Volfson E. Platelet-Poor Plasma for the Treatment of Acute Hamstring Muscle Injuries in Collegiate Football Athletes: A Cohort Study. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2024.
paper.abstract: Twenty consecutive collegiate football players with an acute hamstring injury treated with platelet-poor plasma (PPP) injection from 2021 to 2022 were reviewed. Players returned to full unrestricted sport after an average of 29.4 days, pain improved significantly by 2 weeks after injection, and no recurrent injuries were seen within 12 months. The authors conclude that PPP may be a safe and effective treatment that could expedite return to play.
paper.tldr: In 20 collegiate football players with grade 3b hamstring strains, a platelet-poor plasma injection was followed by return to sport in about a month and no recurrences in a year. Without a comparison group, this is an early, uncontrolled signal rather than proof of benefit.
paper.methods: Retrospective cohort study of 20 consecutive male Division I or III football players with an acute hamstring injury confirmed by ultrasound and graded with a modified BAMIC system. Each player received an ultrasound-guided PPP injection and a standard rehabilitation progression. Outcomes were days to full unrestricted sport, VAS pain, duration of postinjection pain, and recurrence within 12 months, analyzed with descriptive statistics and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
paper.findings: All 20 patients had grade 3b injuries, most often of the semitendinosus (65%). Players returned to full unrestricted sport after a mean of 29.4 days (SD 7.2) following injection, or 34.6 days after the original injury. VAS pain fell from 4.8 before injection to 0.7 at 2 weeks (change 4.1, P<.001) and to 0.0 at 6 weeks. No recurrent injuries were recorded within 12 months, and there were no complications beyond soreness.
paper.limitations: The study is a small, uncontrolled, single-physician series with only grade 3b injuries, male football players and no comparison group. The abstract reports the 29.4-day return as days postinjury, but the Discussion clarifies that 29.4 days is measured from the injection and 34.6 days from the original injury. The article type is labeled Case Report while the design is a retrospective cohort. The authors state that the small sample may not reflect the true recurrence risk. The single treating physician reports a consulting relationship with Lipogems.
paper.practicalImplications: This series alone does not justify adopting PPP injections for grade 3b hamstring strains, because it has no comparison group and cannot separate the injection from rehabilitation and natural healing. The return times and absence of recurrence can be cited as an early, uncontrolled signal in clinical discussions, alongside the authors' call for comparative trials. Findings do not extend to lower-grade injuries, women or non-football athletes.
paper.athleteDev: This study concerns injury treatment rather than training or performance. It does not provide training prescriptions or performance benchmarks, but it may help performance and medical staff discuss expected time away from sport after a grade 3b hamstring strain.
paper.rtp: Use this study to discuss expected return timelines for male collegiate football players with a grade 3b hamstring strain treated with PPP, which were about 29 days after injection in this series. It cannot establish that PPP shortens return to play compared with standard care, and it should not be applied to lower-grade injuries, female athletes or other sports.

records.sourceFile: Multiple Concussions Increase Odds   and Rate of Lower Extremity Injury in National Collegiate Athletic   Association Athletes After Return to Play.pdf

paper.citation: Harada GK, Rugg CM, Arshi A, Vail J, Hame SL. Multiple Concussions Increase Odds and Rate of Lower Extremity Injury in National Collegiate Athletic Association Athletes After Return to Play. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019.
paper.abstract: From 2001 to 2016, 48 NCAA Division I athletes with multiple concussions were matched by sex, sport, position and games played to athletes with a single concussion and to athletes with no concussion history. Lower extremity injury after return to play was more frequent in the multiple-concussion group (75% vs 52% and 56%), and multiple-concussion athletes had higher odds of injury (OR 3.00 vs single concussion; OR 1.66 vs no concussion) and a shorter time to injury. No difference was found between the single-concussion and no-concussion groups.
paper.tldr: Among male collegiate athletes, those with repeated concussions were more likely to be injured in the lower extremity after return to play, and sooner, than matched athletes with one or no concussions. Whether this reflects neuromuscular deficits or player behavior is unresolved.
paper.methods: Retrospective matched cohort study using sports injury records from one NCAA Division I institution. Multiple-concussion athletes were matched to single-concussion and no-concussion athletes by sex, sport, position and games played, and followed for lower extremity injury after return to play until graduation. Odds ratios came from binary logistic regression and time to injury from Kaplan-Meier curves with log-rank tests, censored at 90 days, 1 year and graduation.
paper.findings: Lower extremity injury occurred in 36 of 48 (75%) multiple-concussion athletes, 25 of 48 (52%) single-concussion athletes and 27 of 48 (56%) no-concussion athletes (P=.049). Over the full study period, the multiple-concussion group had higher odds of injury than single-concussion athletes (OR 3.00, 95% CI 1.26 to 7.12) and no-concussion athletes (OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.07 to 2.56), with similar results at 1 year but not at 90 days. Time to injury was shorter in the multiple-concussion group (P=.01), and foot injuries were more frequent in that group (23 vs 4 and 1, P=.001); single-concussion and no-concussion athletes did not differ.
paper.limitations: The sample is small (48 per group) and includes only male athletes from one institution, and 42 of the 48 were football players. The study is retrospective, so records may contain clerical error, and athletes in the multiple-concussion group had to remain in sport long enough to sustain a second concussion. The Results text repeats the full-period ORs (3.00 and 1.66) for the 1-year window, while Table 3 gives 3.06 and 1.83, and the text gives a 1-year log-rank P of .007 while Figure 2 gives .0053. The authors note that player behavior and other confounders could explain the association, although prior lower extremity injury history did not differ between groups.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians and athletic trainers may treat a history of multiple concussions as a marker for closer monitoring of lower extremity injury risk after return to play. The authors suggest that sensitive distal proprioceptive testing may be useful during recovery, although this was not tested. Staff should not assume the association is causal or that it applies to women, other sports or the 90-day window, where no difference was found.
paper.athleteDev: Performance and strength staff may use concussion history as one input when planning workload and monitoring lower extremity injury risk after return to play. The study does not measure training load or performance, so it does not provide training prescriptions.
paper.rtp: Use this study to flag athletes with multiple concussions for closer lower extremity monitoring after return to play, especially in the year after return. It cannot establish that concussion causes lower extremity injury, define a specific clearance protocol, or apply to female athletes.

records.sourceFile: Predictors of early return to sport after surgical repair of proximal hamstring complex injuries in professional athletes - A prospective study.pdf

paper.citation: Lefèvre N, Moussa MK, Valentin E, Meyer A, Bohu Y, Gerometta A, et al. Predictors of Early Return to Sport After Surgical Repair of Proximal Hamstring Complex Injuries in Professional Athletes: A Prospective Study. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2024.
paper.abstract: This prospective cohort of 64 professional athletes who had surgery for a proximal hamstring complex injury (2002 to 2022) assessed return to sport, time to return, quality of return and predictors. Return to sport occurred in 98.4% of athletes, with 78.1% returning to their preinjury competition level at a mean of 6.2 months. Male sex, isolated semimembranosus injury and proximal intratendinous rupture were independent favorable predictors of return at the preinjury level. The complication rate was 4.7%.
paper.tldr: Most professional athletes returned to sport after surgical repair of a proximal hamstring injury, and about 4 in 5 returned to their preinjury level. Male sex, isolated semimembranosus injury and intratendinous rupture were associated with better odds of returning at that level.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort study at a sports surgery referral center, drawn from a registered cohort of professional athletes who had surgical repair of proximal hamstring complex injury. Return to sport was judged against the preinjury level using the Tegner and UCLA activity scales and self-reported performance at 1 year. Univariate and backward-stepwise multivariable Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios for returning at the preinjury level.
paper.findings: Of 64 athletes (82.8% male), 63 (98.4%) returned to sport and 50 (78.1%) returned to their preinjury level at a mean of 6.2 months (SD 2.5). Tegner scores rose from 2.9 before surgery to 8.5 at 1 year (preinjury 8.9), and UCLA scores rose from 3.9 to 9.7 (both P<.0001). Multivariable HRs for returning at the preinjury level were 2.91 for male sex (95% CI 1.01 to 8.35), 3.86 for isolated semimembranosus injury vs all three tendons (95% CI 1.78 to 8.37) and 5.18 for proximal intratendinous rupture vs avulsion (95% CI 2.24 to 12.0). Complications occurred in 3 athletes (4.7%): 1 superficial infection and 2 reruptures.
paper.limitations: The study has no control group, comes from one center and one surgeon, and includes a heterogeneous mix of sports with small subgroups. Return to level was based on activity scales and self-report rather than objective performance, and durability was not documented. The abstract calls the design a case series, while the Methods describe a prospective cohort. Table 4 reports a median delay to surgery of 63 and 81 days, while Table 1 reports a median of 12 days. The volume, issue and page numbers are not printed, so the year is taken from the 2024 copyright line. No athlete with an isolated semimembranosus injury or an intratendinous rupture was in the reduced-performance group, and only 11 athletes were women, so these hazard ratios rest on small or empty cells.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians can counsel professional athletes after surgical repair of a proximal hamstring injury that most will return to sport, and about 4 in 5 will return to their preinjury level, usually near 6 months. Athletes with avulsions involving all three tendons were less likely to return at their preinjury level than those with isolated semimembranosus injuries or intratendinous ruptures, so more cautious expectations are reasonable. Staff should not use the predictors as fixed rules, given the small subgroups.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use the time course and the Tegner and UCLA activity recovery to plan return-to-play milestones for professional athletes after surgery. The study does not measure training loads or performance outputs, so it does not guide training prescription.
paper.rtp: Use this study to set return-to-sport expectations for professional athletes after surgical repair of a proximal hamstring complex injury, with about 6 months to return and about 78% returning at the preinjury level. It cannot establish individual return probabilities or clearance criteria, and it does not apply to non-professional athletes or to nonoperative management.

records.sourceFile: Pain-free vs pain-threshold rehabilitation following acture hamstring strain injury - A randomized controlled trial.pdf

paper.citation: Hickey JT, Timmins RG, Maniar N, Rio E, Hickey PF, Pitcher CA, et al. Pain-Free Versus Pain-Threshold Rehabilitation Following Acute Hamstring Strain Injury: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2020;50(2):91-103.
paper.abstract: Forty-three men with an acute hamstring strain were randomly assigned to pain-free (n=22) or pain-threshold (n=21) rehabilitation with the same standardized exercise and running program. Time from injury to return-to-play (RTP) clearance was the primary outcome, with knee flexor strength, biceps femoris long head (BFLH) fascicle length, fear of movement and reinjury at 6 months as secondary outcomes. Median time to RTP clearance was 15 days (pain-free) and 17 days (pain-threshold), and pain-threshold rehabilitation did not accelerate RTP clearance but produced greater recovery of knee flexor strength and better maintenance of BFLH fascicle length.
paper.tldr: Allowing exercise up to a pain threshold of 4/10 did not speed return to play after a hamstring strain, but it improved knee flexor strength and kept fascicle length gains better at 2 months. Reinjury rates were similar, and the trial was small.
paper.methods: Single-center, double-blind randomized controlled trial in men aged 18 to 40 with an acute posterior thigh injury assessed within 7 days. Participants were stratified by previous hamstring injury and randomized to pain-free or pain-threshold (pain 4/10 or less) rehabilitation, both delivered twice weekly with supervised hamstring strengthening and progressive running. Outcomes were days to RTP clearance (Cox models and Kaplan-Meier curves), isometric knee flexor strength, BFLH fascicle length by ultrasound, Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia, and reinjury over 6 months, analyzed by intention to treat with linear mixed models.
paper.findings: Median time to RTP clearance was 15 days (95% CI 13 to 17) in the pain-free group and 17 days (95% CI 11 to 24) in the pain-threshold group (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.40 to 1.40, P=.37). Isometric knee flexor strength at 90/90 degrees rose by 35% in the pain-free group and 49% in the pain-threshold group, a between-group difference of 15% (95% CI 1% to 28%), while 0/0 strength gains did not differ. BFLH fascicle length gains did not differ at RTP clearance, but the gain from baseline to 2-month follow-up was 0.91 cm greater in the pain-threshold group (95% CI 0.34 to 1.48). Two reinjuries occurred in each group during the 6 months after RTP clearance (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.14 to 7.47, P=1.0).
paper.limitations: Injury was confirmed by clinical assessment only, without MRI, and all participants were men, so findings may not transfer to women or other populations. The sample was small, and the authors note that reinjury data are too limited to draw firm conclusions. Six-month follow-up had missing data (4 pain-free participants could not be contacted), and the 4/10 threshold is an arbitrary choice. The primary outcome is an external, decision-based clearance time and does not report full return to sport. Three of the four reinjuries occurred within 2 months of RTP clearance, raising a possible concern about the clearance criteria. The sample size was calculated for a large effect (effect size 1.2), so the wide confidence interval for RTP time cannot rule out a meaningful difference in either direction.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians may allow progression of eccentric and long-length exercise up to mild pain, at 4/10 or less, without expecting a faster return to play. Choosing a pain threshold may help maintain knee flexor strength and fascicle length, but the reinjury data are too sparse to confirm safety. The authors caution that the RTP criteria may need to account for tissue healing time, given the early reinjuries.
paper.athleteDev: In both groups, eccentric and long-length exercises such as the Nordic hamstring exercise were started in the first session (about 3 days after injury) and progressed by exercise-specific criteria, with large strength and fascicle gains. The pain-threshold group gained more knee flexor strength at 90/90 degrees. The trial does not measure sport-specific performance.
paper.rtp: Use this trial to plan hamstring strain rehabilitation for men with an acute injury, with return-to-play clearance around 2 weeks in both approaches. It cannot show that pain-threshold rehabilitation shortens return to sport, establish safety from the small reinjury numbers, or apply to women, MRI-confirmed injuries or other populations.

records.sourceFile: Pulsed red and blue photobiomodulation for the treatment of thigh contusions and soft tissue injury - A randomized controlled trial.pdf

paper.citation: Wells A, Rigby J, Castel C, Castel D. Pulsed Red and Blue Photobiomodulation for the Treatment of Thigh Contusions and Soft Tissue Injury: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Sport Rehabilitation. 2023.
paper.abstract: Single-blind randomized controlled trial in 44 healthy participants (mean age 21.9 years) who received a standardized quadriceps contusion and then 30 minutes a day for 4 days of an active or placebo pulsed red and blue light patch. The active group improved quadriceps 180°/s peak torque and average power over placebo, and 60°/s average power, but not 60°/s peak torque.
paper.tldr: In a small trial of healthy participants, a pulsed red and blue light patch improved quadriceps strength and power over placebo during 4 days of recovery from an induced thigh bruise. This is short-term evidence from an experimental model, not proof that it speeds real injury recovery.
paper.methods: Single-blinded randomized controlled trial. Healthy participants (23 male, 23 female) had a standardized quadriceps contusion from a tennis-ball machine, then received a 30-minute active or placebo light patch treatment for 4 consecutive days. Isokinetic peak torque and average power at 60°/s and 180°/s were compared with baseline using a mixed-model ANCOVA with sex as a covariate.
paper.findings: The treatment by time interaction favoured the active group for 180°/s peak torque (P = .030) and average power (P ≤ .001). By day 4 the active group was 8.9% and 16.8% above baseline for those measures, while placebo was -1.7% and -2.3%. At 60°/s, average power favoured the active group (P = .041) but peak torque did not differ (P = .704).
paper.limitations: Only isokinetic strength and power were measured; pain, imaging and tissue healing markers were not. Two participants were excluded for protocol noncompliance, leaving 22 per group, effects were assessed only over 4 days, and the 60°/s peak torque result was null. Two of the four authors are affiliated with CareWear Corp, the maker of the tested patch, and the conclusion that clinicians should use it as a standard of care goes beyond a single 44-person trial.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians may consider this light patch as an adjunct for acute thigh contusions when the goal is early strength recovery. The trial supports only short-term isokinetic gains in healthy participants, so it should not replace established care until trials in injured athletes report pain, function and return-to-activity outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: Not directly applicable to performance training. The study measured strength and power recovery after a standardized bruise in healthy participants and did not test performance outcomes in athletes.
paper.rtp: Cannot establish return-to-sport timing. The study measured strength during the first 4 days after an induced contusion and did not measure pain, function, or time to return to activity.

records.sourceFile: MRI findings prior to return to play as predictors of reinjury in professional athletes - A novel decision-making tool.pdf

paper.citation: Isern-Kebschull J, Pedret C, Mechó S, Pruna R, Alomar X, Yanguas X, et al. MRI findings prior to return to play as predictors of reinjury in professional athletes: a novel decision-making tool. Insights into Imaging. 2022;13:203.
paper.abstract: Retrospective observational study of 59 professional athletes with a first acute lower-limb muscle injury and successful rehabilitation, each with MRI within 6 days of injury and within 7 days before return to play. Reinjury occurred in 9 (15.2%). Three control-MRI signs (connective tissue gap, intermuscular oedema, callus gap) were associated with reinjury, and two or more of five signs gave a high-risk classification.
paper.tldr: In 59 male professional athletes, an MRI taken within 7 days before return to play identified who was more likely to be reinjured: those with two or more of five specific signs. This is a small, unvalidated retrospective study, so use it to prompt a closer return-to-play review, not as a cut-off.
paper.methods: Retrospective study of consecutive first-time acute lower-limb muscle injuries in professional athletes over five seasons. Baseline MRI (within 6 days of injury) and control MRI (within 7 days before return to play) were read blind by three musculoskeletal radiologists using a standard scoring system. Reinjury was defined as recurrence within 2 months after return to play and was compared with Fisher's exact tests and a logistic regression model.
paper.findings: Baseline MRI variables were not associated with reinjury. On the control MRI, a transverse or mixed connective tissue gap (OR 39.2, P = .002), intermuscular oedema (OR 8.17, P = .015) and a callus gap (OR 5.75, P = .046) were associated with reinjury. Athletes with two or more of the five signs were classified high risk (OR 29.58, 95% CI 3.86 to 226.64, P = .001): 6 of 9 reinjured athletes versus 0 of 50 who were not reinjured.
paper.limitations: Only 9 reinjuries occurred, so the high-risk group contains 6 events and the confidence intervals are very wide. The methods set significance at P = .01, yet P = .015 and P = .046 are reported as significant, and Table 4 gives a scar maturity OR of 0.45 with a CI of 1.11 to 1.89 that does not contain the estimate. The authors call it a pilot study, the model was not externally validated, and the study is from one club, with mostly soccer players and few athletes per muscle.
paper.practicalImplications: In a professional squad, staff could review a control MRI within 7 days before return to play after a first acute lower-limb muscle injury. Where a transverse or mixed tendon gap, intermuscular oedema or callus gap is present, or two or more of the five signs are seen, the return decision should be re-examined alongside clinical findings. The study does not show that this review lowers reinjury rates.
paper.athleteDev: Limited application to performance. The study addresses return to competition after a muscle injury and does not measure training load, performance, or the GPS monitoring that was part of rehabilitation.
paper.rtp: Can inform the return-to-play decision by flagging athletes with pre-return MRI signs linked to reinjury. It cannot set a safe return date, it does not support using baseline MRI to predict reinjury, and it has not been validated in women, other sports or other muscles.

records.sourceFile: Return to play and performance after opertive treatment of Achilles tendon rupture in elite male athletes - A scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: LaPrade CM, Chona DV, Cinque ME, Freehill MT, McAdams TR, Abrams GD, et al. Return-to-play and performance after operative treatment of Achilles tendon rupture in elite male athletes: a scoping review. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022.
paper.abstract: Scoping review of 13 studies covering 709 elite male athletes (NBA, NFL, MLB, NCAA football and professional soccer) who had operative repair of an Achilles tendon rupture. Return to play ranged from 61% to 100% across leagues, and NBA players showed reduced performance after return, while other sports showed mixed or no significant change. No studies examined non-operative management in elite athletes.
paper.tldr: Most elite male athletes return to play after surgical repair of an Achilles rupture, but performance after return varies by sport. Basketball players showed the clearest declines, and the evidence covers only the first few seasons after injury.
paper.methods: Scoping review following Arksey and O'Malley and Levac et al. guidance. A single PubMed search (March 2021) identified studies of professional or NCAA Division I athletes in baseball, basketball, American football, hockey or soccer that reported an objective performance measure after Achilles rupture. Thirteen studies were included, and return rates, games, playing time and performance were summarised against preoperative levels and matched uninjured controls.
paper.findings: Return rates after operative repair were 61% to 80% in the NBA, 61% to 73% in the NFL, 71% to 96% in professional soccer, 62% to 100% in MLB, and 93% in NCAA Division I football (defensive players). NBA studies consistently reported significantly lower player efficiency rating after return, while NFL, NCAA football and soccer results were mixed and MLB showed no significant decline. No elite-athlete study of non-operative management was found.
paper.limitations: Only one database was searched and the studies used different performance measures, return definitions and time frames, so results could not be pooled or graded. Most data come from retrospective, publicly available statistics, the review cannot tell complete from partial ruptures or surgical technique, and all athletes were male and mostly from North American leagues.
paper.practicalImplications: When counselling an elite athlete after surgical repair of an Achilles rupture, staff can set expectations that most athletes return to sport, but that performance may fall in explosive sports such as basketball. The review also cites general-population trials showing that plantarflexion strength and calf muscle volume may not fully recover even after surgery, and that surgery carries a higher complication rate, which should be part of that discussion.
paper.athleteDev: Relevant to performance expectations after injury. The review shows that sport demands affect how far performance declines after return, which can inform how load and goals are set for a returning athlete, but it does not test training or performance interventions.
paper.rtp: Can inform return-to-play counselling after surgical repair in elite male athletes, including expected return rates and sport-specific performance risk. It does not support decisions on non-operative management, which has no elite-athlete evidence, and it cannot define a safe return date because return criteria were not standardised across studies.

records.sourceFile: Return-to-Play for Elite Athletes With Genetic Heart Diseases Predisposing to Sudden Cardiac Death.pdf

paper.citation: Martinez KA, Bos JM, Baggish AL, Phelan DM, Tobert KE, Newman DB, et al. Return-to-Play for Elite Athletes With Genetic Heart Diseases Predisposing to Sudden Cardiac Death. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2023;82(8):661-670.
paper.abstract: Multicenter retrospective analysis of 76 NCAA Division I and professional athletes with a sudden-death-predisposing genetic heart disease who were risk-stratified and given formal return-to-play approval at four sports cardiology centers. Most had been initially disqualified, and most who returned did so after shared decision making. Over a mean follow-up of 7 years there was 1 exercise-related and 2 nonexercise-related breakthrough cardiac event and no deaths.
paper.tldr: In a retrospective series of 76 elite athletes with genetic heart disease, most who returned to sport after specialist risk assessment and shared decision making had few cardiac events over about 7 years. This small, self-selected series cannot establish how safe return to sport is for all athletes with these conditions.
paper.methods: Multicenter retrospective review of elite athletes (NCAA Division I, Olympic or professional) diagnosed with a sudden-death-predisposing genetic heart disease between 2000 and 2022 at four centers. Medical records were reviewed for diagnosis, disqualification, the return-to-play process and breakthrough cardiac events, which were summarised descriptively without a comparison group.
paper.findings: Of 76 athletes (mean age at return 19.9 years), 55 (72%) were initially disqualified, and after evaluation and shared decision making 69 of 76 (91%) elected to return and were supported by their organisation, 3 withdrew and 4 remained disqualified. During follow-up there was 1 exercise-related breakthrough cardiac event (1.3%) and 2 nonexercise-related events (2.6%), with no sudden cardiac deaths. Twenty-four athletes played with an implantable defibrillator, 8 of them placed for secondary prevention.
paper.limitations: The cohort is retrospective and small, with no comparison group, and athletes were largely self-referred to tertiary specialist centers, so survivor and selection bias are likely. Contact sports such as football and hockey were underrepresented, the authors state the data cannot estimate event incidence, and follow-up is reported both as 200 cumulative athlete-years and as a mean of 7 years per athlete, which do not agree for 76 athletes. The text and Table 3 describe the circumstances of the breakthrough events inconsistently, and the shared decision-making process was not standardised across the four centers.
paper.practicalImplications: For elite athletes with a sudden-death-predisposing genetic heart disease, the study supports a case-by-case return decision made by a sports cardiologist after full risk stratification, treatment and shared decision making, rather than automatic lifelong disqualification. Staff should confirm an automated external defibrillator is available at all training and competition, and plan ongoing cardiac review, since the study cannot show that return is risk-free.
paper.athleteDev: Limited direct performance relevance. The study addresses sport eligibility after a cardiac diagnosis and does not measure training outcomes or performance, although it does show that many athletes returned to high-dynamic sports.
paper.rtp: Relevant to return to sport after a genetic heart disease diagnosis, not to musculoskeletal return to play. It can inform shared decision making with cardiology specialists, but it does not set clearance criteria, has few contact-sport or female athletes, and cannot show that return is safe for every athlete.
